14:1.headline: Do not cut yourselves, and do not split into factions
14:1.body: The plain sense is a ban on gashing your skin in mourning. The Sifrei also hears אגודה, a group, in the word: do not break into separate factions, but be one band.

sources.quote: לֹא תִתְּנוּ גְדִידָה וְשֶׂרֶט בִּבְשַׂרְכֶם עַל מֵת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁהָאֱמוֹרִיִּים עוֹשִׂין
sources.says: Rashi says it means not to make cuts and gashes in your flesh for the dead, as the Amorites did.

sources.quote: לֹא תִתְגֹּדְדוּ – לֹא תֵעָשׂוּ אֲגֻדּוֹת, אֶלָּא הֱיוּ כֻּלְּכֶם אֲגֻדָּה אַחַת
sources.says: The Sifrei says it means do not form separate groups, but all of you be one group.

sources.quote: אִיקְּרִי כָּאן ״לֹא תִתְגּוֹדְדוּ״, לֹא תֵּעָשׂוּ אֲגוּדּוֹת אֲגוּדּוֹת
sources.says: Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yohanan whether the verse forbids forming separate factions.

14:13.headline: The bird called ראה is named for how far it sees
14:13.body: The Talmud says this bird is called ראה, the seer, because it sees so far. It can stand in Babylon and spot a carcass in the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ רָאָה? שֶׁרוֹאָה בְּיוֹתֵר
sources.says: Rashi says it is called ראה because it sees very well.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ רָאָה? שֶׁרוֹאָה בְּיוֹתֵר
sources.says: Rabbi Abahu says it is called ראה because it sees exceptionally far.

sources.quote: עוֹמֶדֶת בְּבָבֶל וְרוֹאָה נְבֵלָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: A teaching adds that it stands in Babylon and sees a carcass in the Land of Israel.

14:17.headline: When the רחם bird comes, mercy comes
14:17.body: Rabbi Yohanan reads the bird's name from רחמים, mercy: when it comes, mercy comes to the world. Another sage says that if it sits on the ground and whistles, the Messiah is coming.

sources.quote: לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ רָחָם? כֵּיוָן שֶׁבָּא רָחָם בָּאוּ רַחֲמִים לְעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rabbi Yohanan says it is called רחם because when it comes, mercy comes to the world.

sources.quote: וּגְמִירִי דְּאִי יָתֵיב אַאַרְעָא וְשָׁרֵיק – אֲתָא מְשִׁיחָא
sources.says: Rav Bivi says there is a tradition that if it sits on the ground and whistles, the Messiah comes.

14:17.headline: The bird that draws fish out of the sea
14:17.body: The sages read שלך as the bird that draws (שולה) fish out of the sea. When Rabbi Yohanan saw one, he quoted the verse that God's judgments are like the great deep.

sources.quote: הַשּׁוֹלֶה דָּגִים מִן הַיָּם
sources.says: Rashi says it is the bird that draws fish out of the sea.

sources.quote: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, כִּי הֲוָה חָזֵי שָׁלָךְ, אָמַר: ״מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ תְּהוֹם רַבָּה
sources.says: The Talmud says that when Rabbi Yohanan saw a שלך he said, your judgments are a great deep.

14:18.headline: The kind bird, still on the list of forbidden birds
14:18.body: The sages say the stork is called חסידה, the kind one, because it shares its food with its companions. It is still one of the birds the Torah forbids.

sources.quote: לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ חֲסִידָה? שֶׁעוֹשָׂה חֲסִידוּת עִם חַבְרוֹתֶיהָ
sources.says: Rav Yehudah says it is called חסידה because it does kindness with its companions.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ חֲסִידָה? שֶׁעוֹשָֹׁה חֲסִידוּת עִם חַבְרוֹתֶיהָ בִּמְזוֹנוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it is called חסידה because it does kindness with its companions in sharing food.

14:18.headline: The bird with a doubled crest, which fetched the shamir
14:18.body: The Talmud reads דוכיפת as הודו כפות, its glory is folded, meaning its crest is doubled. It adds that this is the bird that brought the shamir for building the Temple.

sources.quote: דּוּכִיפַת, שֶׁהוֹדוֹ כָּפוּת, וְזֶהוּ שֶׁהֵבִיא שָׁמִיר לְבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud says it is called דוכיפת because its glory is folded, and that it brought the shamir to the Temple.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמוֹ דּוּכִיפַת? שֶׁ"הוֹדוֹ כָפוּת" וְזוֹ הִיא כַּרְבָּלְתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is called דוכיפת because its glory is doubled, and its glory is its crest.

14:22.headline: Give a tenth so that you grow rich
14:22.body: עשר, a tenth, sounds like עושר, wealth. The Talmud reads the doubled verb as: give a tenth so that you become rich. Rabbeinu Bahya notes that the verse's words do not literally say wealth.

sources.quote: עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר״ — עַשֵּׂר בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁתִּתְעַשֵּׁר
sources.says: The Talmud says: tithe so that you will become rich.

sources.quote: כִּי בְּעִשּׂוּר הַתְּבוּאָה וְהַבְּהֵמָה תִּרְבֶּה הַתְּבוּאָה וְיִרְבֶּה הַמִּקְנֶה
sources.says: Sforno says that by tithing grain and animals, the grain and the herds will grow.

sources.quote: והנה אין בלשון הכתוב לשון עושר
sources.says: Bahya says the wording of the verse has no word for wealth in it.

14:23.headline: Learn to fear God, or get used to it
14:23.body: Ibn Ezra gives two readings. In Jerusalem people will teach you, or the word means training, like a trained calf, so eating there makes fear of God a habit. He prefers the second.

sources.quote: הטעם כי כאשר תלך אל מקום הכבוד שם ילמדוך וטעם שנית להיות למען תלמד כטעם עגלה מלומדה והטעם רגילות והוא הישר בעיני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means they will teach you there, or else it means habit, like a trained calf, and he thinks the second is right.

sources.quote: תהיה רגיל כמו עגלה מלומדה
sources.says: Chizkuni says it means you will become used to it, like a trained calf.

15:1.headline: Shemittah: the year you let debts drop
15:1.body: Ibn Ezra says the name of the seventh year means letting something drop, as when Jezebel's servants were told 'drop her' (שמטוה) and she fell. In this year a lender lets go of what he is owed.

sources.quote: והטעם כמו שמטוה והניחו' ותפול
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meaning is like 'drop her', letting something go so that it falls.

15:2.headline: 'For He called a release' means the time has come
15:2.body: קרא usually means 'called'. Rashbam says here it means the time for release has arrived, as when a festival is 'called' at its set time.

sources.quote: כלומר: כי הגיע זמן שמטה כמו: מקראי קדש קרא עלי מועד, קראו צום, כלם לשון זמן
sources.says: Rashbam says it means the time of release has come, as in 'holy convocations' and 'proclaim a fast', all words for a set time.

15:6.headline: One letter decides who is the lender and who the borrower
15:6.body: Rashi says this form of the verb makes you the lender; a plainer form would make you the borrower. Ibn Ezra and Rashbam tie it to עבוט, a pledge: you will hold the nations' pledges.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן הַלְוָאָה כְּשֶׁנּוֹפֵל עַל הַמַּלְוֶה נוֹפֵל בִּלְשׁוֹן מַפְעִיל, כְּגוֹן וְהִלְוִיתָ, וְהַעֲבַטְתָּ. וְאִם הָיָה אוֹמֵר וְעָבַטְתָּ הָיָה נוֹפֵל עַל הַלֹּוֶה
sources.says: Rashi says a word for lending in the causative form refers to the lender, and the simple form would refer to the borrower.

sources.quote: והטעם תקחו עבוטו שהוא משכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means you will take his pledge, a security.

sources.quote: תקח משכנותם בעל כרחם
sources.says: Rashbam says you will take their pledges against their will for your loans.

15:7.headline: A hand that opens to give and then snaps shut
15:7.body: Ibn Ezra says תקפץ means to close, as a mouth 'shuts'. Rashi reads the two warnings in this verse as two kinds of people: one who agonizes over whether to give, and one who reaches out his hand and then closes it.

sources.quote: תקפוץ. תסגור וכן קפצה פיה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תקפוץ means to close, as in 'she shut her mouth'.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ לְךָ אָדָם שֶׁמִּצְטַעֵר אִם יִתֵּן אִם לֹא יִתֵּן, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר "לֹא תְאַמֵּץ". יֵשׁ לְךָ שֶׁפּוֹשֵׁט אֶת יָדוֹ וְקוֹפְצָהּ, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר "לֹא תִקְפֹּץ"
sources.says: Rashi says one person is torn over whether to give, so it says 'do not harden'; another stretches out his hand and closes it, so it says 'do not shut'.

15:14.headline: Send him off with a gift worn like a necklace
15:14.body: ענק is a necklace. Rashi says the gift should be like jewelry worn high, so all can see you treated him well; others say it means loading the gift onto his neck. Ibn Ezra links it to 'a necklace for your throat' in Proverbs.

sources.quote: העניק תעניק. לְשׁוֹן עֲדִי בַּגֹּבַהּ וּבְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, דָּבָר שֶׁיְּהֵא נִכָּר שֶׁהֱטִיבוֹתָ לוֹ; וְיֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים לְשׁוֹן הַטְעָנָה עַל צַוָּארוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means an ornament worn high and in plain view, something showing you did him good; some explain it as loading onto his neck.

sources.quote: הטעם עשה לו תפארת מגזרת וענקים לגרגרותיך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means giving him honor, from 'necklaces for your throat'.

15:17.headline: A servant 'forever' goes free at the Jubilee
15:17.body: עולם usually means forever. Rashi says here it means until the Jubilee, since in that year every man returns to his family. Fifty years, he says, can be called עולם.

sources.quote: עבד עולם. יָכוֹל כְּמַשְׁמָעוֹ, תַּ"לֹ "וְשַׁבְתֶּם אִישׁ אֶל אֲחֻזָּתוֹ וְאִישׁ אֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ תָּשֻׁבוּ" (ויקרא כ"ה), הָא לָמַדְתָּ שֶׁאֵין זֶה אֶלָּא עוֹלָמוֹ שֶׁל יוֹבֵל
sources.says: Rashi says 'forever' cannot mean its plain sense, since at the Jubilee every man returns home; it means the 'world' of the Jubilee.

sources.quote: מַגִּיד שֶׁחֲמִשִּׁים שָׁנָה קְרוּיִים עוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says this shows that fifty years are called עולם.

18:3.headline: Arm, cheeks, stomach: the priest's gifts recall Pinchas
18:3.body: Rashi cites interpreters who tie each gift to Pinchas: the arm for the spear in his hand, the cheeks for his prayer, and the stomach for where his spear struck the woman. Ibn Ezra says that in the plain sense these are simply the best cuts.

sources.quote: דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת הָיוּ אוֹמְרִים זְרוֹעַ תַּחַת יַד
sources.says: Rashi says interpreters taught that the arm is in return for the hand of Pinchas that took the spear.

sources.quote: לְחָיַיִם תַּחַת תְּפִלָּה
sources.says: Rashi says the cheeks are in return for his prayer.

sources.quote: וְהַקֵּבָה תַּחַת "הָאִשָּׁה אֶל קֳבָתָהּ"
sources.says: Rashi says the stomach is in return for piercing the woman through her belly.

sources.quote: ועל דרך הפשט כי אלה טובים משאר הבשר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says in the plain sense these parts are better than the rest of the meat.

18:9.headline: Do not learn to do it, but you may learn to understand
18:9.body: Rashi says the verse forbids learning these practices to do them, but you may study them to see how corrupt they are and to teach your children. Bahya adds that the high court had to know even sorcery in order to judge.

sources.quote: אֲבָל אַתָּה לָמֵד לְהָבִין וּלְהוֹרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says you may learn in order to understand and to teach.

sources.quote: לְהָבִין מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם כַּמָּה הֵם מְקֻלְקָלִים
sources.says: Rashi says to understand how corrupt their practices are.

sources.quote: וכן מצינו בשבעים סנהדרין שהיו צריכין להיותם בקיאים בכל החכמות אפילו בחכמת הכשפים
sources.says: Bahya says the seventy judges of the Sanhedrin had to be expert in every field, even in sorcery.

18:10.headline: מעונן: one who reads lucky times, fools eyes, or watches clouds
18:10.body: Rabbi Akiva reads מעונן from עונה, a time: one who says a certain hour is lucky for starting. The sages read it from עין, eye, one who fools the eyes, and Bahya adds a third sense, from ענן, one who reads the clouds.

sources.quote: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר אֵלּוּ נוֹתְנֵי עוֹנוֹת – שֶׁאוֹמְרִים עוֹנָה פְּלוֹנִית יָפָה לְהַתְחִיל
sources.says: Rashi cites Rabbi Akiva: these are people who fix times, saying a certain time is good to begin.

sources.quote: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים אֵלּוּ אוֹחֲזֵי הָעֵינַיִם
sources.says: Rashi cites the sages: these are people who trick the eyes.

sources.quote: מעונן, יש בו שלש משמעיות, לשון עונה, לשון עין, לשון ענן
sources.says: Bahya says מעונן has three senses: from time, from eye, and from cloud.

18:11.headline: A joiner of joinings: the charmer who gathers snakes
18:11.body: חבר means to join. Rashi says this charmer gathers snakes, scorpions or other creatures into one place, Ibn Ezra says it means those who claim to join demons together, and Onkelos translates it as one who mutters spells.

sources.quote: שֶׁמְּצָרֵף נְחָשִׁים אוֹ עַקְרַבִּים אוֹ שְׁאָר חַיּוֹת לְמָקוֹם אֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says he gathers snakes, scorpions or other creatures into one place.

sources.quote: וחבר חבר. אלה האומרים שיחברו השדים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these are people who claim to join the demons together.

sources.quote: וְרָטִין רְטָן
sources.says: Onkelos translates it as one who mutters charms.

18:12.headline: בגלל, because of, heard as a turning wheel
18:12.body: Bahya hears גלגל, a wheel, in בגלל: God turns the wheel of the heavens and overrules the stars to drive these nations out. He cites a similar teaching of the sages about charity: it is a wheel that turns in the world.

sources.quote: מהפך הגלגל ומשדד המזלות להורישם מפניך, וזהו לשון בגלל
sources.says: Bahya says God turns the wheel and overrules the stars to drive them out before you, and this is the meaning of בגלל.

sources.quote: כי בגלל הדבר הזה, גלגל הוא שחוזר בעולם
sources.says: Bahya cites the sages on the verse about charity: because of this thing, it is a wheel that turns in the world.

22:1.headline: Shutting your eyes to a lost animal, and when it is allowed
22:1.body: Rashi says והתעלמת means shutting your eyes as if you did not see the lost animal. By the plain sense the verse forbids this. The sages read the same word as allowing it at times, for example when the task is beneath an old man's dignity.

sources.quote: כּוֹבֵשׁ עַיִן כְּאִלּוּ אֵינוֹ רוֹאֵהוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it means pressing your eyes shut as if you do not see it.

sources.quote: לֹא תִרְאֶה אוֹתוֹ שֶׁתִּתְעַלֵּם מִמֶּנּוּ, זֶהוּ פְּשׁוּטוֹ. וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ אָמְרוּ פְּעָמִים שֶׁאַתָּה מִתְעַלֵּם
sources.says: Rashi says the plain sense is 'do not see it and ignore it', but the sages said there are times you may ignore it.

sources.quote: הָיָה כֹּהֵן וְהִיא בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת, אוֹ שֶׁהָיָה זָקֵן וְאֵינָהּ לְפִי כְּבוֹדוֹ, אוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה מְלָאכָה שֶׁלּוֹ מְרוּבָּה מִשֶּׁל חֲבֵירוֹ, לְכָךְ נֶאֱמַר
sources.says: The Talmud gives the cases: a priest when the animal is in a graveyard, an old man for whom it is beneath his dignity, or when his own work is worth more.

22:5.headline: A man's 'gear' on a woman: clothes, or weapons?
22:5.body: כלי can mean clothing or tools. Rashi says the verse is about a woman dressing like a man to slip in among men. Onkelos translates 'a man's weapons', and in the Talmud Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says it means a woman should not go out to war with weapons.

sources.quote: שֶׁתְּהֵא דּוֹמָה לְאִישׁ, כְּדֵי שֶׁתֵּלֵךְ בֵּין הָאֲנָשִׁים, שֶׁאֵין זוֹ אֶלָּא לְשֵׁם נִאוּף
sources.says: Rashi says it means she should not look like a man so as to go among men, which is only for the sake of adultery.

sources.quote: לָא יְהֵי תִקּוּן זֵין דִּגְבַר עַל אִתְּתָא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: a man's weapons shall not be on a woman.

sources.quote: מִנַּיִן שֶׁלֹּא תֵּצֵא אִשָּׁה בִּכְלֵי זַיִין לְמִלְחָמָה
sources.says: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov learns from this verse that a woman should not go out to war bearing weapons.

22:6.headline: 'If a nest is called before you' means it happens by chance
22:6.body: יקרא usually means 'is called'. Ibn Ezra and Rashbam say here it means 'happens to be', from מקרה, chance. Rashi draws the law: the rule is for a nest you come upon, not one you prepared.

sources.quote: יקרא. כמו נקרא נקראתי והם מגזרת מקרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יקרא is like 'I happened to be there', from the word מקרה, chance.

sources.quote: כי יקרא - יזדמן על ידי מקרה
sources.says: Rashbam says it means that it turns up by chance.

sources.quote: כי יקרא. פְּרָט לִמְזֻמָּן
sources.says: Rashi says the wording excludes a nest that is already prepared, that is, one you own.

22:8.headline: 'The faller' is named before he falls
22:8.body: The verse calls the person 'the one who falls' before anything has happened. Ibn Ezra says he is named for his end, as many words are. Rashi says this man was due to fall anyway, but his death should not come through you.

sources.quote: הנופל. נקרא על שם סופו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the one who falls is named for how he ends up.

sources.quote: רָאוּי זֶה לִפֹּל, וְאַעַ"פִּ כֵן לֹא תִתְגַּלְגֵּל מִיתָתוֹ עַל יָדְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says this man deserved to fall, yet his death should not be brought about through you.

22:9.headline: 'Become holy' here means 'become forbidden'
22:9.body: תקדש usually means 'become holy'. Rashi says it is a word for anything set apart from a person, for good as with a gift to the Temple, or for bad as with something forbidden. Chizkuni reads it as 'become mixed'.

sources.quote: כָּל דָּבָר הַנִּתְעָב עַל הָאָדָם, בֵּין לְשֶׁבַח כְּגוֹן הֶקְדֵּשׁ, בֵּין לִגְנַאי כְּגוֹן אִסּוּר, נוֹפֵל בּוֹ לְשׁוֹן קִדּוּשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says anything kept away from a person, for praise like a holy gift or for disgrace like a ban, can be called קדוש.

sources.quote: תקדש - תאסר כקדשים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means it becomes forbidden like holy things.

sources.quote: פן תקדש פן תתערב
sources.says: Chizkuni says פן תקדש means 'lest it become mixed'.

22:11.headline: Shaatnez read as three steps: combed, spun, twisted
22:11.body: Rashi says שעטנז means a mixture. The Mishnah splits the word into שוע (combed), טווי (spun) and נוז (twisted): only cloth made that way is forbidden. Another sage reads it as נלוז, one who turns his Father in heaven against him.

sources.quote: שעטנז. לְשׁוֹן עֵרוּב. וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ פֵּרְשׁוּ — שׁוּעַ טָווּי וְנוּז
sources.says: Rashi says שעטנז means mixing, and the sages explained it as combed, spun and twisted.

sources.quote: אֵין אָסוּר מִשּׁוּם כִּלְאַיִם אֶלָּא טָווּי וְאָרוּג, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (דברים כב) לֹא תִלְבַּשׁ שַׁעַטְנֵז, דָּבָר שֶׁהוּא שׁוּעַ טָווּי וָנוּז
sources.says: The Mishnah says only spun and woven fabric is forbidden, since שעטנז means something combed, spun and twisted.

sources.quote: נָלוֹז וּמֵלִּיז הוּא אֶת אָבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם עָלָיו
sources.says: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reads it as one who is crooked and turns his Father in heaven against him.

22:17.headline: Spreading the cloth: a real sheet, or a figure of speech?
22:17.body: Rashi says this is a figure of speech: the facts will be made as clear as a clean cloth. In the Talmud, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the words mean what they say, a real cloth. Ramban agrees there is no need to read it as a figure.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי זֶה מָשָׁל, מְחֻוָּרִין הַדְּבָרִים כַּשִּׂמְלָה
sources.says: Rashi says this is a metaphor: the matter is made as clear as a cloth.

sources.quote: וּבוֹרְרִין אֶת הַדָּבָר כְּשִׂמְלָה חֲדָשָׁה. רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר: דְּבָרִים כִּכְתָבָן, שִׂמְלָה מַמָּשׁ
sources.says: The Talmud says witnesses come for each side and make the matter clear like a new cloth, while Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says the words are literal: a real cloth.

sources.quote: וְאֵין צֹרֶךְ, כִּי זֹאת לְפָנִים בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מַכְנִיסִין הֶחָתָן וְהַכַּלָּה לַחֻפָּה
sources.says: Ramban says there is no need for the metaphor, since it was the custom in Israel to bring the couple to the wedding canopy and check.

23:1.headline: Kanaf: a garment's corner, or what it hides
23:1.body: כנף usually means a wing or the corner of a garment. Maimonides, following Ibn Janah, says it can also mean something hidden, so the verse means 'he shall not uncover his father's private matter'.

sources.quote: אמר שהוא נאמר גם במשמעות של הסתר
sources.says: Maimonides cites Ibn Janah that the word is also used in the sense of hiding.

sources.quote: וממנו לדעתי "וְלֹא יְגַלֶּה כְּנַף אָבִיו" (דברים כג,א) – לא יגלה את סתר אביו
sources.says: Maimonides says this verse belongs to that sense: he shall not uncover what his father keeps hidden.

23:3.headline: Mamzer: the stranger his own family will not own
23:3.body: Ramban reads ממזר as a man made a stranger (זר) to his brothers, because his father will not acknowledge him for shame. He also cites the Jerusalem Talmud, which reads the word as מום זר, 'a strange blemish'.

sources.quote: מַמְזֵר, שֵׁם לְאִישׁ מוּזָר מֵאֶחָיו וְיוֹדְעָיו, שֶׁלֹּא יִוָּדַע מֵאַיִן בָּא
sources.says: Ramban says mamzer is a name for a man estranged from his brothers and acquaintances, whose origin is unknown.

sources.quote: הוּא יַרְחִיק אוֹתוֹ וְלֹא יוֹדֶה בּוֹ לְבָשְׁתּוֹ וְלִכְלִמָּתוֹ
sources.says: Ramban says the father keeps him at a distance and will not acknowledge him, out of shame.

sources.quote: אָמַר ר' אַבְהוּ מַהוּ מַמְזֵר מוּם זָר
sources.says: Ramban cites Rabbi Abahu: what is mamzer? A strange blemish.

sources.quote: אמר רבי אבהו מאי ממזר, מום זר
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites the same reading from the Jerusalem Talmud.

23:5.headline: 'Al devar': not only 'because', but 'over the scheme'
23:5.body: על דבר is the usual phrase for 'because of'. Rashi reads דבר here as 'counsel': they are kept out over the plan they made to lead Israel into sin.

sources.quote: עַל הָעֵצָה שֶׁיָּעֲצוּ אֶתְכֶם לְהַחֲטִיאֲכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means: over the counsel they devised against you to make you sin.

23:12.headline: Lifnot erev: as the day turns toward evening
23:12.body: Ibn Ezra reads לפנות as the day turning, so the man bathes before sunset and comes back after it. He says those who denied the rabbis' tradition read it as 'before evening', and calls that empty.

sources.quote: לפנות ערב. כטעם כי פנה היום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the phrase is like 'for the day has turned'.

sources.quote: והמכחישי' אמרו כי לפנות כמו לפני ולא אמרו כלום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the deniers read לפנות as 'before', and that they said nothing of value.

sources.quote: סָמוּךְ לְהֶעֱרֵב שִׁמְשׁוֹ יִטְבֹּל, שֶׁאֵינוֹ טָהוֹר בְּלֹא הֶעֱרֵב הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says he immerses close to sunset, since he is not pure until the sun has set.

23:14.headline: Azenecha: not 'your ear' but 'your weapons'
23:14.body: אזנך looks like 'your ear'. Onkelos, Rashi and Rabbeinu Bahya read it as 'your weapons' (זין) with an extra aleph: the soldier carries a digging peg along with his gear.

sources.quote: וְסִכְּתָא תְּהֵי לָךְ עַל זֵינָךְ
sources.says: Onkelos renders: you shall have a peg with your weapons.

sources.quote: אזנך. כְּמוֹ כְּלִי זַיִן
sources.says: Rashi says אזנך means weapons.

sources.quote: האל"ף נוספת, ובאורו על כלי זין שלך
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the aleph is extra and the word means 'with your weapons'.

23:18.headline: Kedeshah: a woman 'set apart', but not for holiness
23:18.body: קדשה shares its root with 'holy', but Rashi reads it as a woman set apart and made ready for prostitution. Onkelos reads the verse another way: an Israelite woman shall not marry a slave.

sources.quote: מֻפְקֶרֶת מְקֻדֶּשֶׁת וּמְזֻמֶּנֶת לִזְנוּת
sources.says: Rashi says she is a woman left open, set apart and ready for prostitution.

sources.quote: לָא תְהֵי אִתְּתָא מִבְּנַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִגְבַר עָבֵד
sources.says: Onkelos renders: an Israelite woman shall not be the wife of a slave.

sources.quote: שֶׁאַף זוֹ מֻפְקֶרֶת לִבְעִילַת זְנוּת הִיא, מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֵין קִדּוּשִׁין תּוֹפְסִין לוֹ בָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi explains Onkelos: such a union counts as harlotry too, since a slave cannot contract a marriage.

23:20.headline: Neshech: interest is called a 'bite'
23:20.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says interest is called נשך, 'bite', from 'if the snake bites'. As venom spreads through the limbs of the one bitten, the punishment spreads into the money of the one who lends at interest.

sources.quote: ונקרא הרבית נשך מלשון (קהלת י׳:י״א) אם ישוך הנחש
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says interest is called neshech from 'if the snake bites' in Ecclesiastes.

sources.quote: כשם שארס הנחש נכנס מן הנושך אל הנשוך באבריו וגידיו, כן עונש האסור נכנס בממונו של מלוה ברבית
sources.says: He says as venom passes from the snake into the limbs of the one bitten, the punishment enters the money of one who lends at interest.

23:25.headline: 'When you come into a vineyard': read as a hired worker
23:25.body: תבא sounds like anyone walking in. Rashi and Onkelos ('when you hire yourself out') say it speaks of a worker hired for the harvest; Rabbeinu Bahya says that otherwise no one could make a living.

sources.quote: בְּפוֹעֵל הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says the verse speaks of a hired worker.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי תִתָּגַר בְּכַרְמָא דְחַבְרָךְ
sources.says: Onkelos renders: when you are hired in your fellow's vineyard.

sources.quote: שאם אתה אומר בביאת כל אדם לא שבקת חיי לכל בריה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says that if it meant anyone who comes in, you would leave no one a living.

24:1.headline: One small word, "because" or "or", changes the divorce law
24:1.body: Resh Lakish says כי has four meanings. The school of Shammai reads it as "because" she did something indecent. Rabbi Akiva reads it as "or also", so a man may divorce even if he simply found another woman more beautiful.

sources.quote: ״כִּי״ מְשַׁמֵּשׁ בְּאַרְבָּעָה לְשׁוֹנוֹת – אִי, דִּלְמָא, אֶלָּא, דְּהָא
sources.says: Resh Lakish says כי has four meanings: if, perhaps, rather, and because.

sources.quote: וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא סָבַר: ״כִּי מָצָא בָהּ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר״ – אִי נָמֵי, מָצָא בָהּ עֶרְוַת דָּבָר
sources.says: The Talmud explains that Rabbi Akiva reads כי here as "or also".

sources.quote: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ מָצָא אַחֶרֶת נָאָה הֵימֶנָּה
sources.says: Rabbi Akiva says he may divorce even if he found another woman more beautiful.

24:1.headline: A "document of cutting" must cut every tie
24:1.body: The divorce paper is called ספר כריתת, "a document of cutting". Rabbeinu Bahya says the name sets the rule: the document must cut her off from him completely, with no strings left for the rest of her life.

sources.quote: ע"ד הפשט הספר הזה כורת בינו לבינה שלא תהא אגודה עמו בשום דבר כל ימי חייה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the document cuts between him and her, so she stays bound to him in nothing for all her life.

24:2.headline: "Another man": a different kind of man from the first
24:2.body: The verse calls her second husband אחר, "another". The Talmud and Rashi read the word as "different": the first man sent a wicked wife out of his house, the second brought her in.

sources.quote: הַכָּתוּב קְרָאוֹ ״אַחֵר״, לוֹמַר: שֶׁאֵין זֶה בֶּן זוּגוֹ לָרִאשׁוֹן – זֶה הוֹצִיא רְשָׁעָה מִבֵּיתוֹ, וְזֶה הִכְנִיס רְשָׁעָה לְתוֹךְ בֵּיתוֹ
sources.says: The Talmud says Scripture calls him "another" because he is not like the first: one removed a wicked woman from his house, the other brought her in.

sources.quote: אֵין זֶה בֶּן זוּגוֹ שֶׁל רִאשׁוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says this man is not the equal of the first.

24:3.headline: The verse predicts how the second marriage ends
24:3.body: The verse says the second husband "hates her" or "dies". Rashi reads it as a forecast, not a case: he will come to hate her, and if not, she will bury him.

sources.quote: הַכָּתוּב מְבַשְּׂרוֹ שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לִשְׂנֹאתָהּ, וְאִם לָאו קוֹבַרְתּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says Scripture tells him he will end up hating her, and if not, she will bury him.

24:5.headline: The new husband must make his wife happy
24:5.body: ושמח could be read "he shall be happy with his wife". Rashi insists it means "he shall make his wife happy", and says a translation that reads it the first way is wrong.

sources.quote: יְשַׂמֵּחַ אֶת אִשְׁתּוֹ, וְתַרְגּוּמוֹ "וְיַחְדֵי יָת אִתְּתֵהּ", וְהַמְתַרְגֵּם וְיֶחְדֵּי עִם אִתְּתֵהּ טוֹעֶה הוּא
sources.says: Rashi says it means he shall gladden his wife, and one who translates "rejoice with his wife" is mistaken.

24:15.headline: The worker risks his life, or sets his hopes, on his wage
24:15.body: The worker "lifts his soul" to his wage. Rashi reads it as risking his life for it, climbing ramps and trees. Rashbam reads it as longing: he is counting on that money to eat.

sources.quote: אֶל הַשָּׂכָר הַזֶּה הוּא נוֹשֵׂא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת, עָלָה בַכֶּבֶשׁ וְנִתְלָה בְאִילָן
sources.says: Rashi says for this wage he risks his life, climbing a ramp and hanging from a tree.

sources.quote: מתאוה נפשו כדי לאכול שכרו
sources.says: Rashbam says his soul longs to eat from his wage.

24:16.headline: Not put to death "for" children: for their sin, or by their word?
24:16.body: The plain reading is that parents are not killed for their children's sins. Onkelos and Rashi read על as "on the word of": a parent is not convicted by a child's testimony. The end of the verse already covers the first meaning.

sources.quote: בְּעֵדוּת בָּנִים, וְאִם תֹּאמַר בַּעֲוֹן בָּנִים, כְּבָר נֶאֱמַר איש בחטאו יומתו
sources.says: Rashi says it means by the testimony of children, since "for the sin of children" is already covered by "each man for his own sin".

sources.quote: לָא יְמוּתוּן אֲבָהָן עַל פּוּם בְּנִין
sources.says: Onkelos translates: fathers shall not die by the mouth of sons.

24:19.headline: Blessed even for the good you did by accident
24:19.body: A farmer who forgets a sheaf must leave it for the poor, "so God will bless you". Rashi notes he did this good by accident and is still blessed. So even a coin someone drops, that a poor man finds, brings a blessing.

sources.quote: וְאַעַ"פִּ שֶׁבָּאת לְיָדוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בְמִתְכַּוֵּן, קַ"וָ לָעוֹשֶׂה בְמִתְכַּוֵּן. אֱמֹר מֵעַתָּה נָפְלָה סֶלַע מִיָּדוֹ וּמְצָאָהּ עָנִי וְנִתְפַּרְנֵס בָּהּ — הֲרֵי הוּא מִתְבָּרֵךְ עָלֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says the blessing comes even when the good was unintended, all the more when intended, so one who drops a coin a poor man lives on is blessed.

24:20.headline: Don't strip the olive tree of its glory, or its branches
24:20.body: תפאר is unusual. Rashi reads it from פאר, "glory": do not take the tree's glory, so leave its corner for the poor. Ibn Ezra reads it from פארות, "branches": do not search the branches. Rabbeinu Bahya adds a sermon: do not boast over the poor.

sources.quote: לֹא תִטֹּל תִּפְאַרְתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ (חולין קל"א), מִכָּאן שֶׁמַּנִּיחִין פֵּאָה לָאִילָן
sources.says: Rashi says do not take away its glory, and learns from here that one leaves a corner of the tree for the poor.

sources.quote: לא תחפש הפארות והם הסעיפים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means do not search the branches.

sources.quote: אל תתפאר על העניים אם אתה מיטיב להן ומניח זיתים תחת האילן
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites a midrash: do not boast over the poor when you do them good and leave olives under the tree.

25:2.headline: 'By number' joins the next word, so forty lashes become thirty-nine
25:2.body: Rashi notes that במספר is read together with ארבעים, 'forty', at the start of the next verse. So it means a count that comes up to forty, not forty itself: thirty-nine lashes.

sources.quote: לומר במספר ארבעים ולא ארבעים שלמים, אלא מנין שהוא סוכם ומשלים לארבעים
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'by the number forty': not a full forty, but a count that leads up to forty.

sources.quote: ארבעים במספר, מנין שהוא סוכם את הארבעים
sources.says: The Sifrei says 'forty by number' means a count that reaches toward forty.

25:3.headline: Once punished, the 'wicked man' is called 'your brother'
25:3.body: Until now these verses call him הרשע, the wicked one. Rashi notes that once he has been lashed, the Torah calls him אחיך, your brother.

sources.quote: כל היום קוראו רשע, ומשלקה קראו אחיך
sources.says: Rashi says the Torah calls him wicked until he is lashed, and then calls him your brother.

sources.quote: אבל מאחר שקבל דינו קוראו אחיך
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says that after he has received his punishment, the verse calls him your brother.

25:5.headline: A verb that undoes its own noun: ויבמה ends her widow status
25:5.body: The verb comes from יבם, the brother-in-law who must marry his brother's widow. Chizkuni says it is one of the words that also mean their reverse, so here it means he removes her status as his brother's widow. Sforno says from then on she is fully his wife.

sources.quote: ויבמה מתבות שיש בה שני פנים בפרושם זה למפרע מזה
sources.says: Chizkuni says ויבמה is one of the words with two opposite meanings.

sources.quote: פירוש יעביר ויסיר היבום ותהיה אשתו
sources.says: Chizkuni says it means he removes the bond to the dead brother and she becomes his wife.

sources.quote: יסיר אותה מהיות עוד יבמתו, אבל תהיה כאשתו לכל דבר
sources.says: Sforno says he takes away her status as his brother's widow, and she is his wife in every way.

25:9.headline: Spit 'in his face', or on the ground in front of him?
25:9.body: בפניו can mean 'in his face' or 'before him'. Rashi, following the rabbis, says she spits on the ground before him. Ibn Ezra says the tradition reads it as 'before him', and offers a plain reading tied to the shoe.

sources.quote: וירקה בפניו. על גבי קרקע
sources.says: Rashi says she spits on the ground.

sources.quote: מפורש בדברי הקבל' שהוא כמו לפניו ודרך הפשט לפני הנעל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the tradition explains it as 'before him', and the plain sense is before the shoe.

25:9.headline: 'Will not build': once he refuses, he cannot change his mind
25:9.body: The verse says יבנה, 'will not build', not בנה, 'did not build'. Rashi learns that once a man has refused and the shoe was removed, he may not later marry her. Rabbeinu Bahya hears in 'build' a link to kindness, as in 'the world is built on kindness'.

sources.quote: כיון שלא בנה — שוב לא יבנה
sources.says: Rashi says that since he did not build, he may not build again.

sources.quote: וזה לשון יבנה כלשון (תהלים פט) עולם חסד יבנה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the word 'build' here echoes 'the world is built on kindness' in Psalms 89.

25:18.headline: Amalek 'tailed' Israel: struck the weak at the back
25:18.body: ויזנב comes from זנב, tail, and appears only twice. Ibn Ezra says Amalek cut off Israel's tail, the weak who fell behind. Rashi brings a midrash that reads it as a 'tail blow' that mocked Israel's circumcision.

sources.quote: ויזנב בך. כרת זנבך והם הנחשלי' אחריך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means he cut off your tail, the stragglers behind you.

sources.quote: מכת זנב, חותך מילות וזורק כלפי מעלה
sources.says: Rashi says it was a tail blow: they cut off circumcisions and threw them upward.

25:19.headline: The passage begins with 'remember' and ends with 'forget'
25:19.body: Rabbeinu Bahya notes that the Amalek passage opens with זכור, remember, and closes with תשכח, forget. He reads it as a hint that one day Amalek's memory will be forgotten from the world.

sources.quote: והפרשה הזו התחילה בזכרון וסיימה בשכחה, להורות שעתיד זכרם להשתכח מן העולם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the passage starts with remembering and ends with forgetting, to show their memory will one day be forgotten.

28:4.headline: שגר: calves the cow 'sends out' from her womb
28:4.body: Rashi reads שגר as newborn cattle. He takes it from the verb 'to send out', since the mother sends them out of her body.

sources.quote: וַלְדוֹת בְּקָרְךָ, שֶׁהַבְּהֵמָה מְשַׁגֶּרֶת מִמֵּעֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means the young of your cattle, which the animal sends out of its womb.

28:4.headline: Flocks called עשתרות because they make their owners rich
28:4.body: Rashi quotes the sages: flocks are called עשתרות because they make their owners rich, מעשירות. They also hold their owners up, like the strong rocks called עשתרות.

sources.quote: לָמָּה נִקְרָא שְׁמָם עַשְׁתָּרוֹת? שֶׁמַּעֲשִׁירוֹת אֶת בַּעֲלֵיהֶן
sources.says: Rashi quotes the sages that the flocks are called עשתרות because they enrich their owners.

28:6.headline: Coming in and going out: each day, or a whole life?
28:6.body: Ibn Ezra reads it as every coming and going: trade, war, daily errands. Rashi reads it as birth and death: may you leave the world as free of sin as when you came in.

sources.quote: או בכל ביאה ויציא' בכל יום ויום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may mean every coming and going, each and every day.

sources.quote: שֶׁתְּהֵי יְצִיאָתְךָ מִן הָעוֹלָם בְּלֹא חֵטְא כְּבִיאָתְךָ לָעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means your leaving the world will be without sin, like your coming into it.

28:20.headline: מארה: not only a curse, but a loss that shrinks things
28:20.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra read מארה here as 'lack': things getting less. Bekhor Shor says the same of ארור: as 'blessed' means plenty, 'cursed' means loss.

sources.quote: המארה. חִסָּרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says מארה means lack, as in the 'spreading' plague of Leviticus.

sources.quote: המארה. המגרע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מארה means diminishing.

sources.quote: כך ארור לשון חסרון והפסד
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says ארור is the language of lack and loss.

28:20.headline: המגערת: used once, read as a 'rebuke' on the crops
28:20.body: This word appears only here. Rashbam reads it from Malachi, 'I will rebuke your seed': God rebukes the crops so they do not grow. Bekhor Shor also offers that everyone will scold you and push you away.

sources.quote: המגערת - הנני גוער לכם את הזרע
sources.says: Rashbam links it to 'I will rebuke the seed for you'.

sources.quote: הכל יגערו בך וירחיקוך מעליהם
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says everyone will rebuke you and keep you away, or else God rebukes the crops.

28:23.headline: Copper sky, iron ground: a softer curse than in Leviticus
28:23.body: Leviticus says the sky will be iron and the ground copper. Rashi says Moses swapped them to soften the curse: copper 'sweats', so the sky still gives some moisture, and iron ground will not rot the crops.

sources.quote: הֵקֵל מֹשֶׁה בְקִלְלוֹתָיו לְאָמְרָן בִּלְשׁוֹן יָחִיד. וְגַם כֵּן בִּקְלָלָה זוֹ הֵקֵל
sources.says: Rashi says Moses softened his curses, and softened this curse too.

sources.quote: שֶׁיִהְיוּ שָׁמַיִם מַזִּיעִין, אַעַ"פִּ שֶׁלֹּא יָרִיקוּ מָטָר
sources.says: Rashi says the sky will sweat a little even if it does not pour rain.

28:25.headline: זעוה: a word with two letters swapped, meaning terror
28:25.body: Rashi reads it as terror, from זוע, 'tremble': everyone who hears of your blows will shake. Ibn Ezra says two letters trade places here, as in כבש and כשב, both meaning lamb.

sources.quote: לְאֵימָה וּלְזִיעַ, שֶׁיָּזוּעוּ כָּל שׁוֹמְעֵי מַכּוֹתֶיךָ מִמְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says it means terror and trembling: all who hear of your blows will tremble.

sources.quote: לזעוה. הפוך כמו כבש כשב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the letters are reversed, as with כבש and כשב.

28:27.headline: חרס: a sore dry as pottery, or a blow from the sun?
28:27.body: Rashi says חרס is a dry sore, hard like a clay shard. Rabbeinu Bahya offers that חרס can mean the sun, as in Job, so this is sunstroke. Ibn Ezra says it is simply the name of an illness, with no other use.

sources.quote: חרס. שְׁחִין יָבֵשׁ כַּחֶרֶס
sources.says: Rashi says it is a boil dry like a potsherd.

sources.quote: אבל יתכן לפרש ובחרס מלשון שמש
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it can be read as 'sun', a blow from the sun.

sources.quote: והנכון שהוא שם חולי כנזכרי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is that it is the name of an illness, like the others listed.

28:30.headline: A coarse word written, a gentler one read aloud
28:30.body: The text writes ישגלנה, a crude word linked to שגל, 'concubine'. Rashi says Scripture replaces it with the politer ישכבנה, 'lie with her', when it is read aloud.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן שֵׁגַל, פִּלֶגֶשׁ, וְהַכָּתוּב כִּנָּהוּ לְשֶׁבַח ישכבנה
sources.says: Rashi says the word comes from שגל, a concubine, and Scripture replaced it with the more decent ישכבנה.

sources.quote: ישגלנה. כנוי לשכיבה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ישגלנה is a term for lying with a woman.

28:32.headline: Eyes that wear out waiting for children who never return
28:32.body: Rashi says these eyes keep watching for the children to come back, and they do not. Any hope that never arrives, he says, is called כליון עינים, the eyes wearing out.

sources.quote: מְצַפּוֹת אֲלֵיהֶם שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ וְאֵינָם שָׁבִים; כָּל תּוֹחֶלֶת שֶׁאֵינָהּ בָּאָה קְרוּיָה כִּלְיוֹן עֵינַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says the eyes wait for them to return and they do not; every hope that does not come is called the wearing out of the eyes.

sources.quote: וכלות לשון כלתה נפשי
sources.says: Chizkuni links it to 'my soul longs', the language of yearning.

28:38.headline: The locust that finishes things off, and how it got its name
28:38.body: Rashi says יחסלנו means 'will finish it off'. That is why one kind of locust is called חסיל: it eats everything up. Ibn Ezra also links it to the חסיל locust.

sources.quote: יְכַלֶּנּוּ, וְעַל שֵׁם כָּךְ נִקְרָא חָסִיל, שֶׁמְּכַלֶּה אֶת הַכֹּל
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'will finish it', and that is why the חסיל is named so: it finishes everything.

sources.quote: והוא מן חסיל מין ממיני הארבה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from חסיל, a kind of locust.

28:42.headline: יירש: will the locust take your trees, or make you poor?
28:42.body: Rashi reads יירש from רש, 'poor': the pest will leave you poor of fruit. He argues it cannot mean 'inherit' or 'drive out', since those would be spelled differently. Rabbeinu Bahya and Onkelos read it as 'drive out'.

sources.quote: יַעֲשֶׂנּוּ הָאַרְבֶּה רָשׁ מִן הַפְּרִי
sources.says: Rashi says the locust will make it poor of fruit.

sources.quote: וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְפָרֵשׁ יְיָרֵשׁ לְשׁוֹן יְרֻשָּׁה
sources.says: Rashi says יירש cannot be read as inheriting, nor as driving out, because of its spelling.

sources.quote: להוריש גוים וכן תרגומו יתרך
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya reads it like 'to drive out nations', as Onkelos translates 'will drive out'.

28:42.headline: צלצל: a buzzing locust, or a clanging enemy army?
28:42.body: Rashi says צלצל is a kind of locust. Ramban thinks it names the enemy army, called for the clang of its war cries and horns, as in צלצלי תרועה in Psalms. Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner and must be read from its place.

sources.quote: צלצל. מִין אַרְבֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says צלצל is a kind of locust.

sources.quote: וְיוֹתֵר נִרְאֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה צְלָצַל שֵׁם לְמַחֲנֶה הָאוֹיֵב
sources.says: Ramban says it seems more likely that צלצל is a name for the enemy camp.

sources.quote: וְיִקָּרֵא הַחַיִל צְלָצַל, בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁיַּשְׁמִיעוּ קוֹל מִלְחָמָה בַּמַּחֲנֶה
sources.says: Ramban says the army is called צלצל because it makes the noise of war.

sources.quote: אין לו ריע ופירושו כפי מקומו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner and its meaning comes from its context.

28:54.headline: The 'soft' man: spoiled by comfort, or tender of heart?
28:54.body: Rashi first reads רך as pampered, used to fine things. His second reading, which Kli Yakar takes, is soft-hearted and kind. Hunger will make even that gentle man cruel to his own family.

sources.quote: הוּא הָרַךְ הוּא הֶעָנֹג — לְשׁוֹן פִּנּוּק
sources.says: Rashi says רך and ענג are the same: being pampered.

sources.quote: הָרַחֲמָנִי וְרַךְ הַלֵּבָב מֵרֹב רַעֲבָנוּת יִתְאַכְזְרוּ
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: the merciful and soft-hearted will become cruel from great hunger.

sources.quote: הָרַכּוּת שֶׁהִזְכִּיר אֵינוֹ רַכּוּת שֶׁל עֹנֶג אֶלָּא רַכּוּת הַלֵּב
sources.says: Kli Yakar says this softness is not of pleasure but of the heart.

28:57.headline: שליה: her youngest children, or the afterbirth itself?
28:57.body: Rashi reads שליתה as her small children. Rashbam says that by the plain sense it is the afterbirth, the word the Talmud uses. Ibn Ezra calls it the place where the baby sits in the womb.

sources.quote: ובשליתה. בָּנֶיהָ הַקְּטַנִּים
sources.says: Rashi says it means her small children.

sources.quote: ובשליתה - שליא ממש כמו שמצינו בתלמוד, לפי הפשט
sources.says: Rashbam says by the plain sense it is an actual afterbirth, as the word is used in the Talmud.

sources.quote: הוא מקום הולד בשבתו בבטן אמו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the place of the baby while it sits in its mother's womb.

28:59.headline: 'Faithful' plagues: true to their mission, or long-lasting?
28:59.body: Rashi says the plagues are נאמנות, faithful: they carry out the job they were sent for. Rashbam says the word means lasting and firm. Bekhor Shor adds that, like a friend's wounds, they are meant to bring you back.

sources.quote: לְיַסֶּרְךָ, לְקַיֵּם שְׁלִיחוּתָן
sources.says: Rashi says they are faithful to punish you and carry out their mission.

sources.quote: ונאמנים - ארוכים ומקוימים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means long-lasting and enduring.

sources.quote: והכוונה לשוב להטיבך ולהחזירך למוטב
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says their purpose is to turn back and do you good, to return you to the right way.

28:63.headline: God does not rejoice at the ruin. He makes others rejoice
28:63.body: The verse says ישיש, not ישוש. Bekhor Shor, citing the Talmud, says this form means God does not rejoice in punishment but causes others to. Rashi reads it the same way: God will make your enemies glad.

sources.quote: ישוש לא נאמר אלא "ישיש" דהוא אינו שש בפורעניות, אבל אחרים משיש
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says it does not say ישוש but ישיש: God does not rejoice in punishment, but makes others rejoice.

sources.quote: כן ישיש ה'. אֶת אוֹיְבֵיכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says God will make your enemies rejoice over you.

28:66.headline: A life that 'hangs': in danger, or living off the market?
28:66.body: Rashi says anything in doubt is called 'hanging': you will not know if you will live through the day. The sages read it as a man who must buy his grain at the market, with no field of his own.

sources.quote: עַל הַסָּפֵק, כָּל סָפֵק קָרוּי תָּלוּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means in doubt, since every doubt is called 'hanging'.

sources.quote: וְרַבּוֹתֵינוּ דָרְשׁוּ זֶה הַלּוֹקֵחַ תְּבוּאָה מִן הַשּׁוּק
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as one who buys grain from the market.

28:67.headline: Wishing for evening: tonight, or last night back?
28:67.body: Rashi says you will wish for last evening back, since each hour is worse than the one before. Rashbam reads it simply: like the sick, you will long for the coming evening, and then for morning.

sources.quote: וְיִהְיֶה הָעֶרֶב שֶׁל אֶמֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says you will wish it were last night's evening.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט: ערב העתיד לבא, שכן דרך החולים
sources.says: Rashbam says by the plain sense it is the coming evening, as is the way of the sick.

28:68.headline: You will try to sell yourselves, and no one will buy
28:68.body: Rashi and Ibn Ezra say והתמכרתם does not mean others will sell you. It means you will offer yourselves as slaves and still find no buyer. Sforno reads it as trying to sell your work to make a living.

sources.quote: אַתֶּם מְבַקְשִׁים לִהְיוֹת נִמְכָּרִים לָהֶם לַעֲבָדִים וְלִשְׁפָחוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says you will seek to be sold to them as slaves.

sources.quote: והתמכרתם. אינו כמו ונמכרתם רק פירושו אתם תבקשו למכור עצמכם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is not 'you will be sold' but 'you will seek to sell yourselves'.

sources.quote: שֶׁתִּשְׁתַּדְּלוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת מִינֵי מְלָאכוֹת לְהִתְפַּרְנֵס בָּהֶן
sources.says: Sforno says you will try to do all kinds of work to earn a living.

29:3.headline: Why only 'until this day' did they understand?
29:3.body: Rashi heard that on this day Moses gave the Torah scroll to the Levites, and all Israel protested that it was theirs too, which made Moses glad. Rabbeinu Bahya cites the sages: a student fully grasps his teacher's mind only after forty years.

sources.quote: אַף אָנוּ עָמַדְנוּ בְסִינַי וְקִבַּלְנוּ אֶת הַתּוֹרָה וְנִתְּנָה לָנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says the people told Moses: we too stood at Sinai and received the Torah, and it was given to us.

sources.quote: הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה הֵבַנְתִּי שֶׁאַתֶּם דְּבֵקִים וַחֲפֵצִים בַּמָּקוֹם
sources.says: Rashi says Moses answered: today I understand that you cling to God and want Him.

sources.quote: מכאן דרשו רז"ל שאין אדם עומד על דעת רבו עד ארבעים שנה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the sages learned from here that no one grasps his teacher's mind until forty years.

29:10.headline: Woodcutters among the people: outsiders who joined by a trick
29:10.body: Rashi says Canaanites came to join Israel in Moses' time, the way the Gibeonites later came to Joshua by a ruse. Moses made them woodcutters and water carriers.

sources.quote: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁבָּאוּ כְנַעֲנִיִּים לְהִתְגַּיֵּר בִּימֵי מֹשֶׁה כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁבָּאוּ גִּבְעוֹנִים בִּימֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
sources.says: Rashi says Canaanites came to convert in Moses' days, just as the Gibeonites came in Joshua's days.

sources.quote: וּנְתָנָם מֹשֶׁה חוֹטְבֵי עֵצִים וְשׁוֹאֲבֵי מַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says Moses made them woodcutters and water drawers.

29:11.headline: To 'pass into' the covenant, not to 'pass over' it
29:11.body: עבר can mean to break a law. Rashi says here it means walking between the halves of cut animals, the old way of making a covenant, and Rabbeinu Bahya notes the verse says 'into' the covenant, so it means entering it.

sources.quote: הָיוּ כוֹרְתֵי בְרִיתוֹת עוֹשִׂין מְחִצָּה מִכָּאן וּמְחִצָּה מִכָּאן וְעוֹבְרִים בֵּינְתַּיִם
sources.says: Rashi says those making covenants set up halves on each side and passed between them.

sources.quote: העברה זו היא הכנסה בברית, כי לא אמר לעברך על ברית אבל אמר בברית
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says this passing means entering the covenant, since it says 'in the covenant', not 'over' it.

sources.quote: ומזה תרגם אונקלוס לאעלותך בקיימא
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says this is why Onkelos translates: to bring you into the covenant.

29:16.headline: Idols named for dung and vermin
29:16.body: The verse calls the idols שקוצים and גלולים. Rashi says the first name means disgusting like creeping vermin, and the second means foul like dung, גלל.

sources.quote: גלליהם. שֶׁמֻּסְרָחִים וּמְאוּסִין כַּגָּלָל
sources.says: Rashi says they are called גלולים because they stink and are loathsome like dung.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהֵם מְאוּסִים כַּשְּׁקָצִים
sources.says: Rashi says שקוצים is their name because they are loathsome like vermin.

29:16.headline: Wood and stone idols out in the open, gold ones locked away
29:16.body: Rashi notices the order of the verse. The wooden and stone idols were seen in public, since no one fears they will be stolen, while the silver and gold ones were 'with them', hidden in inner rooms.

sources.quote: אוֹתָן שֶׁל עֵצִים וְשֶׁל אֲבָנִים רְאִיתֶם בַּגָּלוּי, לְפִי שֶׁאֵין הַגּוֹי יָרֵא שֶׁמָּא יִגָּנְבוּ
sources.says: Rashi says you saw the wood and stone idols openly, because their owner did not fear they would be stolen.

sources.quote: אֲבָל שֶׁל כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב עמהם, בְּחַדְרֵי מַשְׂכִּיתָם הֵם
sources.says: Rashi says the silver and gold ones were 'with them', in their private chambers.

29:18.headline: Following 'what my heart sees'
29:18.body: שררות is a rare word, often read as stubbornness. Rashi links it to Balaam's 'I see him, but not near', so the man says: I will do whatever my heart sees fit.

sources.quote: בשררות לבי אלך. בְּמַרְאִית לִבִּי
sources.says: Rashi says it means by the sight of my heart.

sources.quote: מַה שֶּׁלִּבִּי רוֹאֶה לַעֲשׂוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it means whatever my heart sees to do.

29:22.headline: Sulfur and salt: what fire eats, and what it cannot
29:22.body: Chizkuni asks why salt is paired with sulfur. Salt stands up to fire better than anything and sulfur burns better than anything: had they kept the Torah they would be like salt, but now its fire consumes them like sulfur.

sources.quote: אין לך דבר עומד בפני האש יותר ממלח ואין לך דבר כלה על יד אש יותר מגפרית
sources.says: Chizkuni says nothing resists fire more than salt, and nothing is consumed by fire more than sulfur.

sources.quote: עכשיו שלא קיימוה האש שהתורה יוצאת ממנו תאכלם כגפרית זה שהאש אוכלתו
sources.says: Chizkuni says that since they did not keep the Torah, the fire it comes from will consume them like sulfur.

29:25.headline: Gods that were not 'allotted' to them, or did them no good
29:25.body: Rashi reads חלק as giving a share: God never gave these gods to Israel as their portion. Onkelos reads it differently: these gods never did them any good.

sources.quote: לֹא נְתָנָם לְחֶלְקָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means He did not give those gods to them as their portion.

sources.quote: וְאֻנְקְלוֹס תִּרְגֵּם "וְלָא אוֹטִיבָא לְהוֹן", לֹא הֵטִיבוּ לָהֶם שׁוּם טוֹבָה
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translates it as: they did them no good at all.

29:27.headline: An oversized letter in 'He cast them out'
29:27.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the ל in this word is written large. Since ל is the tallest letter, he says its size may hint at how high Israel's glory stood before it was thrown down in exile.

sources.quote: למ"ד של וישליכם רבתי, וידוע כי היא הגדולה שבכל האותיות
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the ל of וישליכם is large, and it is known to be the tallest of all letters.

sources.quote: יתכן שירמוז אל המעלה הגדולה הנשאת המושלכת בזמן הגלות
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it may hint at the great, lofty standing that was thrown down in the exile.

32:1.headline: Moses says 'give ear' to the sky, and 'hear' to the earth
32:1.body: Ibn Ezra says האזינו comes from אזן, 'ear': lean your ear in. The Tur and Or HaChaim cite the sages: this word suits something close by, and Moses was close to heaven. Isaiah, who was close to earth, swapped the two verbs.

sources.quote: מלת האזינו מגזרת אזן כאילו אמר הטו אזן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says האזינו comes from אזן, as if to say 'incline your ear'.

sources.quote: לפי שלשון אזנה נופל בדבר הקרוב לאדם ומשה שהיה קרוב לשמים אמר בהם אזנה
sources.says: The Tur says the word for 'give ear' is used for what is near, and Moses, near to heaven, used it for heaven.

sources.quote: מֹשֶׁה שֶׁהָיָה קָרוֹב לַשָּׁמַיִם אָמַר ״הַאֲזִינוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם״
sources.says: Or HaChaim quotes the Sifrei: Moses, who was close to heaven, said 'give ear, O heavens'.

32:2.headline: שעירם: storm winds, or fine thin drops?
32:2.body: This word appears only here. Rashi reads it as storm winds, as Onkelos does: winds make the grass grow, as Torah makes its students grow. Ibn Ezra thinks it means thin, fine rain.

sources.quote: כשעירם. לְשׁוֹן רוּחַ סְעָרָה, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it means storm wind, as Onkelos translates.

sources.quote: אַף דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה מְגַדְּלִין אֶת לוֹמְדֵיהֶן
sources.says: Rashi says words of Torah make those who learn them grow, as winds make grass grow.

sources.quote: כשעירם. הנכון בעיני שהם דקים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right reading is that they are fine, thin drops.

32:2.headline: רביבים: raindrops that shoot down like arrows
32:2.body: Rashi suggests drops are called רביבים because they shoot like arrows, as in רבה קשת, 'archer', said of Ishmael. Ibn Ezra reads it from רב, 'many'.

sources.quote: נִרְאֶה לִי עַל שֵׁם שֶׁיּוֹרֶה כְּחֵץ נִקְרָא רְבִיב
sources.says: Rashi says it seems to him a drop is called רביב because it shoots like an arrow.

sources.quote: וכרביבים. מגזרת רב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra derives רביבים from רב, many.

32:4.headline: Why God is called 'the Rock': firmness, or the source of all
32:4.body: Ibn Ezra says God is a rock because He stands firm forever. Maimonides says צור also means a quarry, where stone is cut from, so calling God צור means He is the source of everything that exists.

sources.quote: וטעם הצור. שהוא עומד תמיד כצור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says God is called the Rock because He always stands firm like a rock.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 16
sources.quote: והוא שם המכרה שכורים ממנו אבני מחצב
sources.says: Maimonides says one meaning of צור is the quarry from which building stones are dug.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 16
sources.quote: לפי המשמעות האחרונה הזו נקרא ה' יתעלה "צור", כי הוא הראשית והסיבה הפועלת לכל מה שזולתו
sources.says: Maimonides says that in this last sense God is called צור, as the beginning and the cause of everything else.

sources.quote: אַעַ"פִּ שֶׁהוּא חָזָק, כְּשֶׁמֵּבִיא פֻּרְעָנוּת עַל עוֹבְרֵי רְצוֹנוֹ, לֹא בְּשֶׁטֶף הוּא מֵבִיא כִּי אִם בְּדִין
sources.says: Rashi says though He is strong, when He punishes He does it by justice, not in a flood of force.

32:6.headline: קנך: God bought you, nested you, and set you right
32:6.body: Rashi hears three words in קנך: God acquired you (קנה), set you in a nest (קן) among the rocks, and put you in order (תקן). Rashbam keeps to the first: He bought you out of slavery.

sources.quote: שֶׁקְּנָאֲךָ, שֶׁקִּנֶּנְךָ בְּקַן הַסְּלָעִים וּבְאֶרֶץ חֲזָקָה, שֶׁתִּקֶּנְךָ בְּכָל מִינֵי תַקָּנָה
sources.says: Rashi says He acquired you, nested you in a nest of rocks, and set you right in every way.

sources.quote: קנך - קנה אותך. שפדאך מבית עבדים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means He bought you, redeeming you from slavery.

32:9.headline: חבל: a measured share of land, and a rope of three strands
32:9.body: Ibn Ezra explains חבל as a portion, since land was measured with a rope. Rashi adds that Jacob, the third patriarch, is like a rope of three strands: his grandfather's merit, his father's, and his own.

sources.quote: חבל. כמו גורל כמו חבלים. כי בחבל ימודו הארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says חבל means a lot or share, because land is measured with a rope.

sources.quote: כַּחֶבֶל הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא עָשׂוּי בְּג' גְּדִילִים
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob is like a rope made of three strands.

32:10.headline: Found in the desert: found faithful, or given enough?
32:10.body: Rashi first reads it as 'found': God found Israel faithful in the desert. He also gives Onkelos's reading, which Rashbam follows: מצא as 'be enough', God supplied all they needed there.

sources.quote: אוֹתָם מָצָא לוֹ נֶאֱמָנִים בְּאֶרֶץ הַמִּדְבָּר
sources.says: Rashi says God found them faithful to Him in the desert.

sources.quote: וְאֻנְקְלוֹס תִּרְגֵּם יִמְצָאֵהוּ — "יַסְפִּיקֵהוּ כָּל צָרְכּוֹ בַמִּדְבָּר"
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translates it 'He supplied all his needs in the desert'.

sources.quote: הקב"ה היה סיפוק שלהם
sources.says: Rashbam says God was their supply.

32:10.headline: אישון: the pupil of the eye, or the eyelid that guards it?
32:10.body: Rashi says the אישון is the dark center of the eye that light comes from. Rashbam and Bekhor Shor say it is the eyelid, which covers and darkens the eye, as in באישון לילה, 'the dark of night'. Either way, God guards Israel as closely as that.

sources.quote: הוּא הַשָּׁחֹר שֶׁבָּעַיִן שֶׁהַמָּאוֹר יוֹצֵא הֵימֶנּוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the black of the eye, from which light comes out.

sources.quote: הוא הבשר שנכפף על העין
sources.says: Rashbam says it is the flesh that folds over the eye, the eyelid.

sources.quote: ועל שהוא מחשיך את העין כשהוא נופל עליו. כמו באישון לילה ואפלה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says it is named for darkening the eye when it closes, as in 'the dark of night'.

32:11.headline: The eagle hovers over its young, touching and not touching
32:11.body: Rashi says the eagle does not press its weight on its chicks: it hovers, touching and not touching. Ibn Ezra links ירחף to מרחפת at the start of Genesis, where God's spirit hovers over the water.

sources.quote: אֵינוֹ מַכְבִּיד עַצְמוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם אֶלָּא מְחוֹפֵף — נוֹגֵעַ וְאֵינוֹ נוֹגֵעַ
sources.says: Rashi says the eagle does not weigh down on them but hovers, touching and not touching.

sources.quote: ירחף. בנסעם מגזרת מרחפת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra derives ירחף from מרחפת, hovering.

32:12.headline: 'Alone': God alone led them, or Israel lived apart?
32:12.body: Rashbam reads בדד as God alone: He by Himself brought them out of Egypt. Ibn Ezra offers a second reading: Israel alone, as in Balaam's 'a people that dwells alone'.

sources.quote: הוא לבדו הוציאם ממצרים
sources.says: Rashbam says God alone took them out of Egypt.

sources.quote: כמו הן עם לבדד ישכון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בדד may refer to Israel, as in 'a people that dwells alone'.

sources.quote: נִהֲגָם בַּמִּדְבָּר בָּדָד וּבֶטַח
sources.says: Rashi says He led them in the desert alone and in safety.

32:15.headline: ישרון: 'the upright one' grew fat and kicked
32:15.body: ישרון is a name for Israel. Ibn Ezra and the Tur read it from ישר, 'upright': the one who was upright grew fat and rebelled. Rabbeinu Bahya reads it from אשורנו, 'I see him', for the people who saw God's glory at Sinai, and says Moses uses this honored name here to shame them.

sources.quote: ויתכן להיות מגזרת ישר והטעם שמן זה שהיה ישר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it may come from ישר: this one who was upright grew fat.

sources.quote: וישמן ישורון. ישראל שהיה ישר
sources.says: The Tur says ישרון is Israel, who was upright.

sources.quote: ויתכן לפרש כי קראם כן לחסרונם כדי להוכיחם ולהכלימם
sources.says: Bahya says Moses may have called them by this name to rebuke and shame them for falling short of it.

32:17.headline: Gods that never made your fathers' hair stand on end
32:17.body: Rashi first reads שערום from שער, 'hair': your fathers never feared these gods enough for their hair to stand up. His second reading, like Rashbam's, takes it from שעירים, goat-demons: your fathers never made such idols.

sources.quote: לֹא עָמְדָה שַׂעֲרָתָם מִפְּנֵיהֶם, דֶּרֶךְ שַׂעֲרוֹת הָאָדָם לַעֲמֹד מֵחֲמַת יִרְאָה
sources.says: Rashi says their hair did not stand up before them, as a person's hair stands up from fear.

sources.quote: שְׂעִירִים הֵם שֵׁדִים, לֹא עָשׂוּ אֲבוֹתֵיכֶם שְׂעִירִים הַלָּלוּ
sources.says: Rashi says שעירים are demons, and your fathers did not make such idols.

sources.quote: לשון לשעירים, אשר הם זונים אחריהם
sources.says: Rashbam reads it from the goat-demons that people strayed after.

32:18.headline: תשי: you forgot the Rock, or you wore down His strength
32:18.body: Rashi and Rashbam read תשי as 'you forgot', from נשה. The sages, Rashi adds, hear התיש, 'weaken': when God comes to do you good, you anger Him and sap His power to help you.

sources.quote: תשי. תִּשְׁכַּח
sources.says: Rashi says תשי means 'you forgot'.

sources.quote: כְּשֶׁבָּא לְהֵיטִיב לָכֶם אַתֶּם מַכְעִיסִין לְפָנָיו וּמַתִּישִׁים כֹּחוֹ מִלְּהֵיטִיב לָכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read it as: when He comes to do you good, you anger Him and weaken His power to do good for you.

sources.quote: תשי - תשכח. מן נשה
sources.says: Rashbam says it means 'you forget', from the root נשה.

32:18.headline: The God who brought you out of the womb
32:18.body: Rashi reads מחללך as the One who brought you out of the womb. He links it to חיל, the pains of a woman giving birth, and Ibn Ezra agrees it may come from that word.

sources.quote: אל מחללך. מוֹצִיאֲךָ מֵרֶחֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means the One who brings you out of the womb, from the word for birth pangs.

sources.quote: ויתכן היות גזרת מחוללך מחיל כמו הרה תקריב ללדת תחיל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says מחללך may come from חיל, as in a pregnant woman about to give birth who writhes in pain.

32:20.headline: אמן: children who did not take their upbringing, or had no faith?
32:20.body: Rashi first reads אמן from אומן, 'one who raises a child': the good upbringing God gave them does not show. His second reading, from Onkelos, is אמונה, 'faith': they promised at Sinai and soon made the golden calf.

sources.quote: אֵין גִדּוּלַי נִכָּרִים בָּהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the way God raised them cannot be seen in them.

sources.quote: אָמְרוּ בְסִינַי נַעֲשֶׂה וְנִשְׁמָע וּלְשָׁעָה קַלָּה בִטְּלוּ הַבְטָחָתָם וְעָשׂוּ הָעֵגֶל
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: at Sinai they said 'we will do and we will listen', and soon broke the promise and made the calf.

32:24.headline: מזי רעב: swollen, hairy, or burnt by hunger?
32:24.body: This word appears only here. Onkelos reads 'swollen with hunger', but Rashi says he has no proof for it. Rashi gives Rabbi Moshe HaDarshan's reading, 'hairy with hunger', from Aramaic מזיא, hair, since a starving body grows hair. Ibn Ezra reads 'burnt by hunger'.

sources.quote: וְאֵין לִי עֵד מוֹכִיחַ עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi says he has no proof for Onkelos's 'swollen with hunger'.

sources.quote: שְׂעִירֵי רָעָב — אָדָם כָּחוּשׁ מְגַדֵּל שֵׂעָר עַל בְּשָׂרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi gives the reading 'hairy from hunger': a starved person grows hair on his body.

sources.quote: מזי רעב. כמו שרופי רעב מגזרת למזא לאתונא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means burnt by hunger, from the Aramaic for heating the furnace.

32:24.headline: מרירי: a demon by name, or the bitterness of a plague?
32:24.body: Rashi reads קטב מרירי as destruction by a demon named Meriri. Ibn Ezra reads it as a bitterness in the air, that is, a plague.

sources.quote: וּכְרִיתוּת שֵׁד שֶׁשְּׁמוֹ מְרִירִי
sources.says: Rashi says it is destruction by a demon named Meriri.

sources.quote: מרירי. מרירות באויר כמו כמרירי יום
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is bitterness in the air, as in 'the bitterness of the day'.

32:26.headline: One word read as three: 'in anger, where are they?'
32:26.body: This word appears only here. The Sifrei, which Onkelos follows, splits אפאיהם into three words, אף אי הם: in My anger I would make them vanish, so people ask 'where are they?'. Rashi also reads it from פאה, to cast them off like abandoned property. Ibn Ezra says it is one word with no partner, meaning 'destroy them'.

sources.quote: הַחוֹלֶקֶת תֵּבָה זוֹ לְשָׁלוֹשׁ תֵּבוֹת, אָמַרְתִּי אַף אֵי הֵם
sources.says: Rashi says the Sifrei, followed by Onkelos, splits this word into three: 'I said: anger, where are they'.

sources.quote: וְיֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ אפאיהם אֲשִׁיתֵם פֵּאָה, לְהַשְׁלִיכָם מֵעָלַי הֶפְקֵר
sources.says: Rashi says it can also mean 'I will make them a corner', casting them off as ownerless.

sources.quote: יש אומרים שהם שלש מלות והנכון שאין לו ריע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says some read three words, but the right view is that it is one word with no partner.

32:27.headline: אגור: the enemy's anger 'gathered up', or a word of fear?
32:27.body: Rashi reads אגור as 'gathered': the enemy's anger is piled up against Israel. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'I fear', notes Onkelos's 'gather', and prefers 'strife'. He adds that the verse speaks in human terms so listeners can understand.

sources.quote: אִם לֹא שֶׁכַּעַס הָאוֹיֵב כָּנוּס עֲלֵיהֶם לְהַשְׁחִית
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'were it not that the enemy's anger is gathered against them to destroy'.

sources.quote: אגור. אפחד מגזרת ויגר מואב והמתרגם אמר מגזרת אגרה בקציר והנכון שהוא מלשון תגרה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אגור means 'I fear', the translator took it as 'gather', and the right sense is 'strife'.

sources.quote: והכתוב דבר כדרך בני אדם להבין השומעים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Scripture speaks in human terms so the listeners will understand.

32:40.headline: 'I raise My hand to heaven': an oath, or My dwelling place?
32:40.body: Rashi first reads the raised hand as an oath, as people raise a hand to swear. In his second reading, יד means 'place', as in איש על ידו, 'each at his place': God keeps His dwelling in heaven.

sources.quote: כִּי בַחֲרוֹן אַפִּי אֶשָּׂא יָדִי אֶל עַצְמִי בִּשְׁבוּעָה
sources.says: Rashi says in His anger God raises His hand to Himself in an oath.

sources.quote: ידי. מְקוֹם שְׁכִינָתִי
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: 'My hand' means the place of My presence.

sources.quote: תָּמִיד אֲנִי מַשְׁרֶה מְקוֹם שְׁכִינָתִי בַשָּׁמַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says God always keeps the place of His presence in heaven.

32:43.headline: וכפר: God comforts His land, or wipes the blood from it?
32:43.body: Rashi reads כפר as 'appease': God will comfort His land and His people for what they suffered. Rashbam reads it as 'wipe clean': the blood spilled on the land is wiped away by the blood of those who spilled it.

sources.quote: וכפר. לְשׁוֹן רִצּוּי וּפִיּוּס
sources.says: Rashi says וכפר means appeasing and comforting.

sources.quote: וכפר אדמתו עמו - יקנח דם עמו מן האדמה על ידי שפיכת דם אויבים
sources.says: Rashbam says God will wipe His people's blood from the land by spilling the enemies' blood.

32:44.headline: Why Joshua is called by his old name, Hoshea
32:44.body: Moses had long ago renamed him Yehoshua. Rashi says the Torah calls him Hoshea here to show he stayed humble: even after he was given greatness, he was the same man as at first. Ibn Ezra says it is simply the name all Israel knew him by.

sources.quote: וְלָמָּה קוֹרְאֵהוּ כָּאן הוֹשֵׁעַ? לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא זָחָה דַעְתּוֹ עָלָיו
sources.says: Rashi asks why he is called Hoshea here and says it shows he did not grow proud.

sources.quote: וקראו הכתוב הושע בשם שהיו כל ישראל יודעין אותו כי מי ידע שכנה שמו מש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Scripture uses the name all Israel knew, since not everyone knew Moses had renamed him.

32:47.headline: If a law seems empty, the emptiness is in you
32:47.body: Rashi says nothing in the Torah is empty: even a line of names teaches something. Rabbeinu Bahya quotes the midrash that reads מכם, 'from you', closely: if a law seems empty, the lack is in your own understanding.

sources.quote: אֵין לְךָ דָבָר רֵיקָן בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁאִם תִּדְרְשֶׁנּוּ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַתַּן שָׂכָר
sources.says: Rashi says there is nothing empty in the Torah that does not carry reward when studied.

sources.quote: ואם רק הוא מכם, כלומר שאם לא נודע לכם טעם הדבר אין החסרון אלא מצד השכל שבכם
sources.says: Bahya quotes the midrash: if it is empty, it is from you; if you do not know a law's reason, the lack is in your own mind.

32:48.headline: 'In the middle of this very day': Moses dies in broad daylight
32:48.body: Rashi notes that בעצם היום הזה appears three times: for Noah, for the Exodus, and here. Each time people said they would stop it, so God did it at midday. Here Israel said they would not let Moses die.

sources.quote: בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁה מְקוֹמוֹת נֶאֱמַר בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
sources.says: Rashi says the phrase 'in the middle of this very day' appears in three places.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל אוֹמְרִים בְּכָךְ וְכָךְ אִם אָנוּ מַרְגִּישִׁין בּוֹ — אֵין אָנוּ מַנִּיחִין אוֹתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says Israel said that if they noticed, they would not let Moses go, so God did it at midday.

33:2.headline: A law of fire: Torah written in black fire on white
33:2.body: The word is written as one, אשדת, and read as two, אש דת, a fire of law. Rashi says the Torah was written before God in black fire on white fire. Onkelos says God gave it out of the fire.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיְתָה כְתוּבָה מֵאָז לְפָנָיו בְּאֵשׁ שְׁחֹרָה עַל גַּב אֵשׁ לְבָנָה
sources.says: Rashi says the Torah was written before God from long ago in black fire upon white fire.

sources.quote: כְּתַב יַמִּינֵיהּ מִגּוֹ אֶשָּׁתָא אוֹרַיְתָא יְהַב לָנָא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: the writing of His right hand, from within the fire, He gave the Torah to us.

sources.quote: התורה שנתנה באש וברק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is the Torah that was given with fire and lightning.

33:3.headline: A word with no partner: gathered at the foot of Sinai
33:3.body: Rashi reads תכו from תוך, inside: Israel placed themselves at the foot of the mountain, at God's feet. Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner, and reports another view: even if beaten for God's sake, they would not leave His words.

sources.quote: שֶׁהֲרֵי תִּוְּכוּ עַצְמָן לְתוֹךְ תַּחְתִּית הָהָר לְרַגְלֶךָ בְּסִינַי
sources.says: Rashi says they put themselves inside the bottom of the mountain, at Your feet, at Sinai.

sources.quote: תכו. בלא אח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says תכו has no partner in the Bible.

sources.quote: כטעם אפילו שיוכו בשבילך לא יעזבו דבריך וזה רחוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports a reading that even if they are beaten for You they will not leave Your words, and calls it far-fetched.

33:4.headline: Not an inheritance, but a bride promised to Israel
33:4.body: מורשה means an inheritance. The Talmud plays on the sound and says to read it as מאורסה, betrothed. It is as if the Torah were a bride promised to Israel, not only something handed down.

sources.quote: אַל תִּקְרֵי: ״מוֹרָשָׁה״, אֶלָּא: מְאוֹרָסָה
sources.says: Rabbi Hiya teaches: do not read it as inheritance but as betrothed.

sources.quote: מורשה הִיא לִקְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב, אֲחַזְנוּהָ וְלֹא נַעַזְבֶנָּה
sources.says: Rashi says it is an inheritance for the congregation of Jacob: we have taken hold of it and will not leave it.

33:12.headline: The Temple sits between Benjamin's shoulders, a little low
33:12.body: Rashi says the Temple was built on high ground in Benjamin's land, but not at the very top. The Talmud says David planned to build it higher, at Ein Eitam, and lowered it a little because the verse says between his shoulders.

sources.quote: בְּגֹבַהּ אַרְצוֹ הָיָה בֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ בָּנוּי, אֶלָּא שֶׁנָּמוּךְ עֶשְׂרִים וְשָׁלוֹשׁ אַמָּה מֵעֵין עֵיטָם
sources.says: Rashi says the Temple was built on the high part of his land, but twenty-three cubits lower than Ein Eitam.

sources.quote: סְבוּר לְמִבְנְיֵיהּ בְּעֵין עֵיטָם – דְּמִדְּלֵי; אָמְרִי: נִיתַתֵּי בֵּיהּ קַלִּיל, כְּדִכְתִיב: ״וּבֵין כְּתֵפָיו שָׁכֵן
sources.says: The Talmud says they thought to build it at Ein Eitam, which is high, but said to lower it a little, as it is written: between his shoulders He dwells.

33:14.headline: Fruit ripened by the moon, or a harvest every month
33:14.body: ירח means both moon and month. Rashi gives both: some crops, like cucumbers and gourds, are ripened by the moon. Or the land pushes out new produce month after month, as Onkelos translates.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ פֵּרוֹת שֶׁהַלְּבָנָה מְבַשַּׁלְתָּן וְאֵלּוּ הֵן קִשּׁוּאִין וּדְלוּעִין; דָּ"אַ — גרש ירחים. שֶׁהָאָרֶץ מְגָרֶשֶׁת וּמוֹצִיאָה מֵחֹדֶשׁ לְחֹדֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says some fruits are ripened by the moon, such as cucumbers and gourds, or else the land puts out produce from month to month.

sources.quote: מֵרֵישׁ יְרַח בִּירַח
sources.says: Onkelos translates: from the start of each month, month by month.

33:17.headline: Joshua gets the ox's strength and the wild ox's horns
33:17.body: Rashi says Moses is blessing Joshua, who came from Joseph. An ox is strong but its horns are plain. A ראם, a wild ox, has fine horns but less strength. Joshua was given both.

sources.quote: שׁוֹר כֹּחוֹ קָשֶׁה, וְאֵין קַרְנָיו נָאוֹת, אֲבָל רְאֵם קַרְנָיו נָאוֹת וְאֵין כֹּחוֹ קָשֶׁה, נָתַן לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ כֹּחוֹ שֶׁל שׁוֹר וְיֹפִי קַרְנֵי רְאֵם
sources.says: Rashi says an ox is strong but its horns are not handsome, and a ראם has handsome horns but is not as strong, and Joshua was given the ox's strength and the beauty of the ראם's horns.

33:18.headline: Zebulun trades at sea so Issachar can study in his tents
33:18.body: Rashi reads the tents as tents of Torah. Zebulun and Issachar made a partnership: Zebulun sailed out to trade and fed Issachar, who sat and learned. That is why Zebulun is named first.

sources.quote: זְבוּלֻן וְיִשָּׂשכָר עָשׂוּ שֻׁתָּפוּת, זְבוּלֻן לְחוֹף יַמִּים יִשְׁכֹּן וְיוֹצֵא לִפְרַקְמַטְיָא בִּסְפִינוֹת וּמִשְׂתַּכֵּר וְנוֹתֵן לְתוֹךְ פִּיו שֶׁל יִשָּׂשכָר, וְהֵם יוֹשְׁבִים וְעוֹסְקִים בַּתּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says Zebulun and Issachar were partners: Zebulun traded by ship and put food in Issachar's mouth, while they sat and studied Torah.

sources.quote: לְפִיכָךְ הִקְדִּים זְבוּלֻן לְיִשָּׂשכָר שֶׁתּוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁל יִשָּׂשכָר עַל יְדֵי זְבוּלֻן הָיְתָה
sources.says: Rashi says this is why Zebulun comes before Issachar, since Issachar's Torah came through Zebulun.

33:19.headline: Treasures hidden in the sand: a snail, a fish, and glass
33:19.body: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner and means hidden things. The Talmud names them: the חלזון snail, a fish called טרית, and white glass from the sand. Rashi says these were found in the land of Zebulun and Issachar.

sources.quote: שְׂפוּנֵי״ — זֶה חִלָּזוֹן, ״טְמוּנֵי״ — זוֹ טָרִית, ״חוֹל״ — זוֹ זְכוּכִית לְבָנָה
sources.says: Rav Yosef teaches that שפוני is the snail, טמוני is the tarit fish, and חול is white glass.

sources.quote: טָרִית וְחִלָּזוֹן וּזְכוּכִית לְבָנָה הַיּוֹצְאִים מִן הַיָּם וּמִן הַחוֹל, וּבְחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל יִשָּׂשכָר וּזְבוּלֻן הָיָה
sources.says: Rashi says the tarit fish, the snail, and white glass come out of the sea and the sand, and were in the portion of Issachar and Zebulun.

sources.quote: ושפני. לְשׁוֹן כִּסּוּי
sources.says: Rashi says ושפני means covering.

sources.quote: ושפוני טמוני חול. אין לו אח וטעמו כמו טמוני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner and means the same as hidden.

33:21.headline: A hidden grave, or a paneled palace
33:21.body: Rashi and Onkelos say Gad's land holds the grave of the lawgiver, Moses, hidden from every creature. Ibn Ezra reads ספון as paneled, like a cedar-lined house, so Gad saw the fine palaces of the Amorite nobles.

sources.quote: אוֹתָהּ חֶלְקָה סְפוּנָה וּטְמוּנָה מִכָּל בְּרִיָּה
sources.says: Rashi says that plot is covered and hidden from every creature.

sources.quote: משֶׁה סָפְרָא רַבָּא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל קְבִיר
sources.says: Onkelos translates that Moses, the great scribe of Israel, is buried there.

sources.quote: והטעם כי ראה ארמונים ספונים שהיו חלק גדולי האמורי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Gad saw paneled palaces that belonged to the Amorite nobles.

33:22.headline: A lion cub leaping, or a river gushing out
33:22.body: Ibn Ezra says יזנק has no partner and pictures Dan as a lion cub leaping from the Bashan. Rashi follows Onkelos: it is the Jordan gushing out in Dan's land, from the cave of Paneas.

sources.quote: יזנק. אין לו חבר במקרא והטעם דמהו בגבורתו לגור אריה כאשר ידלג מהר בשן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner in Scripture, and that Dan is compared to a lion cub leaping from Mount Bashan.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה הַיַּרְדֵּן יוֹצֵא מֵחֶלְקוֹ מִמְּעָרַת פַּמְיָאס
sources.says: Rashi says the Jordan flowed out of Dan's portion, from the cave of Paneas.

sources.quote: אַרְעֵיהּ שָׁתְיָא מִן נַחֲלַיָּא דְּנָגְדָן מִן מַתְנָן
sources.says: Onkelos translates that his land drinks from rivers that flow from the Bashan.

33:25.headline: A word found once: your old age, or your wealth flowing in
33:25.body: דבאך appears only here. Rashi gives two readings: your old age will be as good as your youth, or other lands will pour their silver and gold into yours. Onkelos reads it as your strength, as in the days of your youth.

sources.quote: וּכְיָמִים שֶׁהֵם טוֹבִים לְךָ, שֶׁהֵן יְמֵי תְחִלָּתְךָ, יְמֵי נְעוּרֶיךָ, כֵּן יִהְיוּ יְמֵי זִקְנָתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says that as your good days, the days of your youth, are, so will the days of your old age be.

sources.quote: שֶׁכָּל הָאֲרָצוֹת יִהְיוּ דוֹבְאוֹת כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב לְאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says, in another reading, that all lands will pour silver and gold into the Land of Israel.

sources.quote: וּכְיוֹמֵי עוּלֵמָתָךְ תָּקְפָּךְ
sources.says: Onkelos translates: as the days of your youth, so will your strength be.

sources.quote: וכימיך דבאך. אין לו ריע
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word has no partner.

33:27.headline: God of old is a dwelling place
33:27.body: מענה means a dwelling. Rashi says the ה at the end does the work of a ל at the start: the heavens are a dwelling for the God of old. Ibn Ezra reads it the other way: the eternal God is your shelter.

sources.quote: כָּל תֵּיבָה שֶׁצְּרִיכָה לַמֶ"ד בִּתְחִלָּתָהּ הֵטִיל לָהּ הֵ"א בְּסוֹפָהּ
sources.says: Rashi says any word that needs a ל at its start may take a ה at its end instead.

sources.quote: לְמָעוֹן הֵם הַשְּׁחָקִים לֵאלֹהֵי קֶדֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the heavens are a dwelling for the God of old.

sources.quote: והטע' כי מעונה שלך הוא אלהי קדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means your dwelling is the God of old.

4:7.headline: God is near in knowing, not in distance
4:7.body: The verse calls God קרבים, near, to Israel. Maimonides cites it and says nearness to God is never about place, but about knowing Him.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 18
sources.quote: כי כל אלה קרבת ידיעה, כלומר השגה של ידע, לא קרבת מקום
sources.says: Maimonides says all these verses speak of nearness in knowledge, not nearness in place, and he cites this verse among them.

4:10.headline: The same word means 'learn' and then 'teach'
